title: [1.30.x] HTTP/3 (QUIC) connections leak? Active connections grows unbounded
body: After upgrading from nginx 1.28.x to 1.30.2 on Ubuntu 24.04, stub_status Active connections steadily grows over days or weeks, from roughly 500 to more than 3000, and only a full restart resets it. With HTTP/3 enabled, I measured 445 established TCP connections but 855 Active and 768 Waiting connections. After commenting out the QUIC listeners, removing the Alt-Svc h3 advertisement, and fully restarting nginx, Active tracked established TCP roughly 1:1 and stayed flat; a reload alone did not clear the count. Re-enabling QUIC brings the growing gap back. The configuration uses 64 workers, reuseport QUIC listeners, quic_retry, and nginx built with the HTTP/3 module and OpenSSL 3.0.13.

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from nginx 1.28.x to 1.30.2, stub_status Active connections slowly rises from about 500 into the thousands over days or weeks.
With HTTP/3 enabled I see 855 Active and 768 Waiting while ss reports 445 established TCP connections; after disabling HTTP/3 and fully restarting, Active stays close to the established TCP count.
A reload does not clear the accumulated count, but a full restart does.
N0.label: N0 HTTP/3-associated Active count growth reported

symptoms_visible: After I set worker_shutdown_timeout to 30 seconds, Active connections continue climbing in the same way as before.
N1_x.label: N1_x shutdown-timeout aftermath

symptoms_visible: On nginx 1.30.3, the same Active connection growth continues with HTTP/3 enabled.
The worker PIDs remain the same between checks, but the error log repeatedly reports worker processes exiting on signal 11.
N2.label: N2 repeated worker crashes surfaced

symptoms_visible: Workers continue to segfault while HTTP/3 is enabled, and Active connections continue to accumulate.
Two coredumps have the same stack through BUF_MEM_grow_clean, SSL handshake handling, and ngx_ssl_handshake.
N3.label: N3 coredump evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After I rebuilt nginx against OpenSSL 4.0 and deployed it in production, the Active connection growth and worker crashes disappeared.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved after moving off the OpenSSL 3.0 QUIC compatibility configuration

solution.intent: Treat the rising shared Active count as the result of old worker generations lingering after reloads, and force those workers to exit by configuring worker_shutdown_timeout.
solution.concrete_example: Set worker_shutdown_timeout 30s, reload nginx, and check whether old worker generations exit and the Active count returns to baseline.

edges.comment: From participant1 c1 and reporter c2-c3, on the reporter's nginx system: the initial lingering-shutdown-worker theory led the reporter to keep worker_shutdown_timeout 30s configured, but the same continuous growth remained.

question_patterns: What exact nginx build and loaded dynamic modules are you running now?
Please share the current nginx -V output and the contents of the modules directory.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have switched to the official nginx repository and am now running nginx 1.30.3 on Ubuntu 24.04, built with OpenSSL 3.0.13 and --with-http_v3_module. I no longer have the GPS module; the loaded dynamic modules are Brotli and Zstandard filter/static modules.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I am still using a third-party nginx build with a custom module that replaces TLS or QUIC handling.
The build is otherwise identical, but only the Brotli modules are loaded and the Zstandard modules are absent.

question_patterns: Can you periodically run ps -o pid,etimes,stat -C nginx and see whether old worker generations remain?
Do the worker PIDs change or show workers older than the most recent reload?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran ps -o pid,etimes,stat -C nginx about once an hour. The PIDs seemed to remain the same and their elapsed times kept growing.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Each reload leaves another complete generation of old worker PIDs in a shutting-down state for hours.

question_patterns: Are there worker crashes, alerts, or unusual errors in the nginx logs while the count grows?
Please check the error log for worker exits or signals.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The log has many alerts saying worker processes exited on signal 11. They continue after the latest full restart; I do not see another relevant error around them.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There are no worker exits, signals, restarts, or other errors during the entire period in which Active grows.
The same signal 11 alerts occur, but at a slightly lower frequency.

edges.comment: From participant1 c4's requests and reporter c5, all describing the original reporter's deployment. The reporter had independently moved to the official 1.30.3 package and removed the earlier GPS module, creating persistent system state S2; the process checks and log review are measurements.

question_patterns: Can you install the debug symbols and provide a GDB backtrace from one of the worker coredumps?
Please inspect the repeated SIGSEGV coredumps and paste the raw stack and relevant buffer fields.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I installed the nginx debug symbols and inspected two recent coredumps. Both have the same stack: __memset_avx512_unaligned_erms, BUF_MEM_grow_clean in libcrypto, an SSL library frame, ngx_ssl_handshake, ngx_ssl_handshake_handler, and the epoll worker loop. In the caller frame, s->init_buf appears to have length 4294967808 while max is 21848. I pasted the full dump and attached the summary screenshot; I only have a slight clue what it means.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every coredump instead points into a Brotli response-filter function, with no SSL handshake or QUIC frames present.
The same BUF_MEM_grow_clean and ngx_ssl_handshake stack appears, but the corrupted length has a different large pointer-like value.

edges.comment: From reporter c6-c7 on the reporter's own production system. The answer preserves the raw GDB stack and field values. Determining why the counters rise and whether nginx or OpenSSL originated the corruption remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Avoid the crashing HTTP/3 compatibility configuration: either disable HTTP/3 while using the system OpenSSL 3.0.x package, or rebuild nginx against a QUIC-capable OpenSSL release using the native API, then verify under the same production traffic.
solution.concrete_example: For the stock Ubuntu 24.04-linked package, remove the QUIC listeners and Alt-Svc h3 advertisement so clients fall back to HTTP/2. If HTTP/3 is required, use a custom nginx build against OpenSSL 3.5.1 or newer; the reporter rebuilt against OpenSSL 4.0 and reported that the problem disappeared.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied signal-11 logs, raw coredump stacks, and corrupted BUF_MEM fields. Engineers inferred that crashed workers leave their connection contributions undecremented in the shared stub_status counters. The thread initially attributed the crash to OpenSSL itself, but the final technical follow-up explicitly walked that certainty back: SSL_do_handshake may be only the delayed victim of heap corruption, and changing to a newer OpenSSL also changes nginx from its compatibility shim to the native QUIC API. The accepted operational diagnosis is therefore the crashing HTTP/3/OpenSSL-compatibility configuration, not a conclusively proven bad write in OpenSSL alone.

edges.comment: From participant1 c8-c15 and reporter c16-c17. This follows the opening reporter's own deployment only. The final remediation remained OpenSSL 3.5.1+ for HTTP/3 or disabling HTTP/3 on 3.0-3.4; the reporter then rebuilt with OpenSSL 4.0 and confirmed the problem disappeared in production.

solution.intent: Recognize the known HTTP/3 compatibility configuration and move away from it by disabling HTTP/3 on the system OpenSSL build or rebuilding nginx against a TLS library with native QUIC support, followed by production verification.
solution.concrete_example: Since disabling QUIC already keeps the count flat, leave HTTP/3 disabled on the stock system-OpenSSL package or rebuild nginx against OpenSSL 3.5.1 or newer, then monitor worker crashes and stub_status under the same traffic.

edges.comment: Shortcut copy of the accepted operational remedy so an agent that immediately proposes the correct safe mitigation can match from the start. It skips the later evidence that distinguishes stale counters after crashes from the initial lingering-worker theory.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify that the rising stub_status Active value is not a true unbounded QUIC connection leak: repeated worker crashes leave connection counts undecremented in the shared status counters, so only a full restart clears them.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the observed signal-11 worker exits, the repeated BUF_MEM_grow_clean-to-ngx_ssl_handshake coredump stack, the QUIC enable/disable comparison, and the failure of worker_shutdown_timeout to change the behavior.
Must not present worker_shutdown_timeout as the fix; the reporter tried 30 seconds and the same continuous growth remained.
Must recommend avoiding HTTP/3 on the system OpenSSL 3.0.x compatibility configuration or rebuilding nginx against a TLS library with native QUIC support.

Must not overstate the final root cause as conclusively proven to be an OpenSSL-only defect: the thread's final technical assessment says the handshake crash may be a delayed victim of heap corruption and the original bad write was not located.

Must ask the reporter to verify under representative real traffic that worker crashes stop and stub_status remains stable before declaring resolution; the reporter ultimately confirmed the problem disappeared after rebuilding with a newer OpenSSL.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced production nginx operator who can rebuild nginx, modify QUIC listeners, compare socket and stub_status metrics, inspect processes and logs, install debug symbols, and collect GDB data, but does not confidently interpret low-level C/OpenSSL internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, cooperative, and evidence-driven; supplies commands, configurations, logs, coredumps, and follow-up measurements, while candidly noting when low-level debugging output is beyond their expertise.
